R07-E-01: When a person pushes a door that should have been pulled, the usual verdict is that the person was careless, and the verdict is so automatic that we rarely notice how strange it is. A door has one job that involves its user, which is to tell an approaching hand what to do, and a door that sends the wrong message has failed at that job as surely as a door that sticks in its frame. Yet the failure is booked to the person, who apologises and blushes, while the door goes on misleading everyone who comes after. The habit of blaming users has a simple source, which is that designers judge their objects from the inside. They know which way the door swings because they drew it, and they know which button on the oven sets the timer because they chose its position. What is obvious to someone who already knows the answer tells us very little about what an object communicates to someone meeting it for the first time, in a hurry, with a bag in one hand. A flat plate invites pushing and a vertical bar invites pulling, whatever the small sign above them says. When the hardware and the sign disagree, people follow the hardware, and they are not foolish to do so, since the shape of a thing is read faster than words are. There is a practical cost to the blaming habit beyond the irritation it causes. Errors that are attributed to individuals are treated by asking individuals to try harder: more signs, more training, more warnings printed in red. Errors that are attributed to design are treated by changing the design, which removes the error for everyone at once. Imagine a hospital in which two different medicines are supplied in bottles of the same size and colour. If it blames the nurse who confuses them, it may discipline that nurse and still find the confusion repeated next year by someone else; if it makes the bottles look different, it removes the occasion for the mistake altogether. This is not to say that every mistake is the designer's fault, or that objects can be made so clear that nobody ever misuses them. Some tasks are intrinsically demanding, and some carelessness is simply carelessness. But the sensible default runs the other way from the usual one. When many people make the same mistake with the same object, the repetition is itself a kind of evidence, and it points less at the people than at the thing they all share.
R07-E-02: Admirers of vernacular building, the houses and barns put up by people who were not architects, often describe them as stores of climatic wisdom. The thick earth walls of a desert village keep rooms cool through the afternoon and release their stored warmth at night; the steep roofs of a snowy valley shed their load before it can crush the rafters; the raised floors of a flood plain let the water pass beneath. Each form, on this account, is the answer a community reached after centuries of trial, and modern builders, with their sealed glass boxes and mechanical cooling, would do well to copy it. There is much truth in this, but the story is told too kindly. The forms that survive to be admired are the ones that worked well enough to be kept; the failures, the houses that collapsed and the villages abandoned after a bad decade, left nothing for us to photograph. What we see is therefore a filtered record, and it flatters the past. More important, vernacular forms were shaped by poverty and scarcity as much as by climate. People built with earth because earth lay underfoot and cost nothing to carry, not because they had compared it with every other material and found it best. A thick wall may be cool, but it may also be dark, damp in the rains and laborious to patch every year, and those who lived behind it bore those costs whether or not their admirers mention them. None of this makes vernacular building less worth studying. It suggests, however, that the lesson lies in the method rather than in the forms. What village builders did well was to adjust slowly and continuously to the conditions in front of them, keeping what worked and changing what did not, with materials whose behaviour they knew intimately because they handled them every season. Their knowledge was local by necessity, and its strength was precisely that it never pretended to be anything else. A modern builder who copies the outward shape of a courtyard house in a different climate, with different materials and a different way of living, has learned nothing from it, however picturesque the result. One who studies local sun, wind and rain with the same patience, builds, watches what happens and is willing to revise, has learned a great deal, even if the building that results looks nothing like a village house.
R07-E-03: For much of the last century it was an article of faith among progressive architects that ornament was a kind of lie. A building, they argued, should declare its structure and its purpose plainly; carving and moulding added cost without adding use, and they disguised what a building really was beneath a costume borrowed from some other age. The argument had moral force, and it produced buildings of great clarity. It also rested on a narrow idea of what counts as use. Consider what ornament has traditionally done: a carved surround tells a stranger which of many openings is the entrance, so that nobody needs to read a sign to find the way in. A band of moulding at the level of the first floor breaks a tall wall into parts that a human eye can measure, so that a passer-by senses the height of the building in storeys rather than as an undifferentiated cliff. Projecting mouldings over windows throw rain clear of the glass and, as they weather, gather their stains in a pattern that reads as intended rather than as decay. Even purely figurative ornament, a row of leaves or a face above a door, offers the eye something to rest on at walking pace, which is the pace at which most people meet most buildings. These are uses, though not of the kind that appear in a structural calculation. The critics were right about one thing: ornament applied without regard to any of these purposes, stuck on to a facade like a label on a jar, is as dishonest as they said, and much commercial building of their day was exactly that. But the remedy they chose, to strip surfaces bare, threw away the work along with the pretence. A blank wall is not neutral, for it tells the stranger nothing about where to go in, it offers no measure of scale, and it weathers into streaks that look like neglect because nothing in its design anticipated them. The plain building is honest about its structure and silent about almost everything else that a person on the street needs to know. The more useful question, then, is not whether a building should be ornamented but what its ornament is for. Asked in that way, the question rules out a good deal of pastiche, the reproduction of historical detail for its associations alone. It also rules out a good deal of austerity that passes itself off as rigour, and it returns the judgement of a facade to the people who have to find their way past it.
R07-E-04: A curious reversal has taken place in the market for handmade goods. For most of history, the aim of a skilled potter or weaver was regularity: bowls that stacked, threads of even thickness, a pattern that repeated without drift. Irregularity was the mark of an apprentice or of a hurried job, and the master's pride lay in eliminating it. Today, by contrast, the small wobble in a glaze or the slight lean of a hand-thrown cup is what many buyers are paying for. It has become the proof that a person, and not a machine, was involved. The trouble with this proof is that it can be forged. A machine that can make a perfect cup can be programmed to make an imperfect one, and to vary the imperfection from piece to piece so that no two look alike. Tableware with deliberately uneven rims and glazes is already produced in quantity, and an ordinary buyer cannot tell it from the real thing. If what we value in the handmade is irregularity as such, then the handmade has no defence against its imitation, and the premium paid for it is a premium paid for a story. But irregularity was never the point, and treating it as the point misunderstands what a craftsperson does. A turner working a piece of wood meets a knot, a change in the grain, a softer patch, and alters the cut to suit it; a weaver feels the tension of the warp change with the damp in the air and corrects for it. The handmade object is the record of many such small judgements, each a response to the particular material in front of the maker. Its variations, where they occur, are traces of that responsiveness, not ornaments added afterwards. A machine-made irregularity, however convincing, responds to nothing; it is a pattern generated in advance and imposed on material treated as uniform. This distinction can be pressed too far. Machines can be built to sense and respond to their material, and a good deal of hand production is as mechanical as anything in a factory, the same motion repeated on identical parts without a thought. The line between craft and its imitation, then, is not drawn by the presence of a hand. It is drawn by whether the making involved attention to the particular, and by that test some machine work would count as craft while much of what is sold as handmade would not.
R07-E-05: Every few generations someone tries to rescue a dying craft by writing it down. A retiring stonemason or bell founder is interviewed at length, his methods are photographed and measured, and the results are published as a manual that, it is hoped, will allow the craft to survive its last practitioners. The manuals are often admirable documents, careful, accurate and lovingly illustrated. They are also, as anyone who has tried to learn from one discovers, strangely inert: the reader can follow every step and still produce work that a practitioner would reject at a glance. The reason is that much of what a skilled worker knows is not a set of steps at all but a way of perceiving. A smith judges the heat of iron by its colour, and the relevant differences of colour are ones that a novice literally does not see; a joiner hears in the note of a mallet whether a joint has seated; a plasterer feels through the trowel the moment at which the mix has begun to stiffen. Such judgements can be described, but the description presupposes the perception it describes. An instruction to work the metal when it turns the colour of straw is useful only to someone who already knows which straw, in which light, and how much variation is allowed. Apprenticeship solved this problem not by explaining more but by arranging for the learner to perceive under guidance. The apprentice stood beside the master for years and was told 'now' and 'not yet' thousands of times, until he slowly came to see what the master saw. The words mattered, but chiefly as pointers to experiences the learner was having at that very moment. What passed from one generation to the next was less a body of information than a trained attention. It would be sentimental to conclude that apprenticeship should simply be restored. It was slow, it was often exploitative, and the guilds that ran it guarded their knowledge as much to keep out competitors as to preserve standards. Nor are manuals useless: to a learner who has already begun to see, a good written account can organise and extend what practice has started. The lesson is narrower. A craft cannot be stored in a text in the way a recipe can, because what has to be preserved is a capacity of persons, and the only reliable way to keep it alive is to keep people practising it alongside others who already can.
R07-E-06: When an old building is to be repaired, those responsible must first decide what, exactly, they are repairing it to. One answer, long popular and still widely held, is that the building should be returned to its original state, or to the state its first builders intended. Later additions are stripped away, missing parts are reconstructed from evidence or from informed guesses, and the result is a building more complete and more consistent than it has been for centuries. The appeal is obvious: the visitor sees the church or the fort as it was meant to be seen, whole and coherent. The opposing answer holds that a building's history does not stop at its completion. A medieval hall that later acquired a Georgian window, a Victorian staircase and a twentieth-century kitchen is a document of all those periods, and to strip it back to its first state is to erase most of what it records. On this view the repairer's duty is to keep what has survived, to intervene as little as possible, and to make any new work distinguishable from the old, so that no one mistakes a modern guess for an original fact. The restored building, by contrast, presents the restorer's idea of the past as though it were the past itself. I find the second answer more persuasive, but it is not as neutral as its defenders sometimes suggest. Not every layer is worth keeping: a cheap partition put up in a hurry may hide a painted ceiling of real importance, and refusing to remove it is itself a choice about which history matters. Keeping everything is also an interpretation, one that values continuity over quality and treats the accident of survival as a kind of verdict. The conservator, no less than the restorer, decides what the building will say. What separates the two approaches, then, is not that one interprets and the other does not. It is that conservation, at its best, leaves its interpretations visible and reversible, so that a later generation with better evidence or different priorities can undo them. Restoration tends to make its choices permanent and to conceal them, since a convincing reconstruction is one in which the seams cannot be found. Because every generation has been confident about the past and most have been wrong about some of it, the approach that allows its mistakes to be corrected deserves the benefit of the doubt.
R07-E-07: Most people who hold opinions about celebrated modern buildings have never been inside them. They know them from photographs, and the photographs share a family resemblance. They are taken in the weeks after completion, before the occupants have moved in, on a day chosen for its light. Furniture, if there is any, is placed by the photographer; people, if they appear at all, are small and blurred, present to give scale rather than to show use. The building is caught at the single moment when it most resembles its architect's intention and least resembles the place it will become. There is nothing sinister in this. The photographer is paid to show the work at its best, as a portrait painter is, and an empty room displays its proportions more clearly than a crowded one. The difficulty lies in what happens when such images become the principal medium through which architecture is judged. Reputations are made in magazines and, increasingly, on screens, and they are made quickly, long before anyone knows whether the roof leaks, whether the offices overheat in summer, or whether the grand atrium is a pleasure to cross on a wet Monday morning. Critics, who seldom have the time or the budget to return, write from the same images, and the first account of a building tends to become the account that is repeated. A building's reputation is thus fixed at the very moment when least is known about it. The effect is not confined to critics. Architects are not naive about how their work will be seen, and a profession whose rewards follow the photograph will tend, without anyone deciding it, to design for the photograph. Qualities that register in a single frame, a dramatic cantilever, a pure white surface, a striking silhouette against the sky, come to be favoured over qualities that can be experienced only over time or through the other senses: the way a staircase feels under tired feet, the acoustics of a dining room, the dignity with which a material ages. White render photographs beautifully and often weathers badly; a brick that looks dull on the day of opening may look better in its fiftieth year than in its first. Defenders of the photograph reply that it is the only way most of us can see buildings in distant cities, and that the alternative, judging only what one has personally visited, would make criticism parochial. They add that many buildings which photograph well also work well, and that architects idealised their work in drawings long before the camera existed. Each of these points is fair, yet none of them reaches the central point. The complaint is not that photographs flatter, which drawings did too, but that the moment of photographing has become the moment of judgement, and that the qualities a photograph can register have quietly become the qualities that count. One modest remedy would be to make the second look as normal as the first. A building photographed and discussed again after ten years of use, with its occupants in it and its materials weathered, would be judged on evidence that the opening day cannot supply. Such a practice would not abolish the glamour of the new, and it is not meant to. It would simply give the slower virtues of a building a chance to be seen by those who will never walk through it, and it would give architects a reason to care about the tenth year as much as the first, since that is when they would next be judged.
R07-E-08: Architects tend to speak of a building as finished on the day it is handed over, and most architectural criticism shares the assumption. For its occupants, however, the handover is a beginning. Within a few years the first partitions have gone up or come down, a porch has been enclosed, a garage has become a bedroom, and the building has started to diverge from its drawings. A family grows and then shrinks, a business expands into the floor above, a school changes the way it teaches, and each of these shifts leaves its mark on the fabric. Over a century the divergence can be so complete that little of the original arrangement survives except the outer walls and the structural frame. If we want to know how well a building has been designed, the question of how it absorbs such changes deserves at least as much attention as the question of how it looked when new. The obvious response is to design for change, and for several decades architects attempted exactly that. Offices and schools were built as open floors with movable partitions, and houses with walls that could slide, fold or be unbolted, so that occupants could rearrange the interior at will. The results were often disappointing. Movable partitions were seldom moved, because moving them was laborious and disturbed the services concealed within them; the flexible plan turned out to be a plan that suited no particular use well; and the occupants, rather than enjoying their freedom, filled the space with improvised screens and cabinets to make the rooms that the design had declined to provide. Designing for every possible use, it emerged, had been a way of designing for none. The buildings that have in fact proved most adaptable are frequently ones that were never designed with change in mind. Old warehouses and mills, with their regular grids of columns, generous ceiling heights and thick, plain walls, have been turned into flats, studios, schools and offices with surprising ease. Terraced houses built for one family have been divided into apartments and, a generation later, joined up again. What these buildings share is not flexibility in the engineered sense but a kind of slack: dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe. The ordinary builder called in to knock two rooms together can see at once where the loads run and what may safely be taken away. They fit their first use loosely, and that looseness is what lets them fit their later uses at all. The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision. A building tailored exactly to its brief, every room sized to its programme and every service routed to suit it, is admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter, because the brief will change and the building cannot. Generosity of this kind costs something at the outset, in floor area and in height, and clients are seldom eager to pay for space that nobody has yet asked for. This is not an argument against all precision; an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely, and a little slack in the wrong place is merely waste. But for most ordinary buildings, which will outlive the purposes for which they were commissioned, the more durable virtue is a certain generosity, together with a willingness on the architect's part to regard the occupants' later alterations not as defacement but as the building continuing to do its job.
